Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 449 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

I agree with my principal's decision that every student should take part in at least one extracurricular activity. School is about more than passing tests, and the hours after the final bell are often where students learn the things a classroom cannot teach.

The first reason is that activities help students build real skills. A student who works on the yearbook has to meet deadlines, take photographs, write captions, and cooperate with a team of editors. If one person misses a deadline, the whole book is late. That kind of responsibility is hard to learn from a worksheet. Students on the student council learn something similar. They plan a fall dance, set a budget, and argue politely about whether to spend money on a DJ or on decorations. These are the same skills adults use at work every day.

The second reason is that activities help students find a place to belong. Many teenagers feel lost at a big school, especially in ninth grade. When I was new at my school, I did not know anyone, and I spent lunch alone for weeks. Then a friend talked me into joining the cross-country team. Within a month I had a group of people to sit with, and I looked forward to practice. Students who feel connected to a school tend to attend more often and to care more about their grades. A required activity gives every student a chance at that connection, including the shy ones who would never sign up on their own.

Some people argue that a requirement is unfair because certain students have jobs or must care for younger siblings. That is a fair concern, but it can be solved without throwing out the rule. The school can offer activities that meet during lunch or in short sessions, and it can count some kinds of community service or club work done outside school. The rule should be flexible, but it should still exist. Without it, the students who most need a place to belong are the ones most likely to stay away.

Others say that students already have too much homework. Yet research and everyday experience both suggest that students who stay active often manage their time better, not worse. A busy schedule forces a person to plan. Many athletes and band members finish their homework faster because they know practice is coming.

In the end, a requirement for one activity is a small ask with a large reward. It pushes students to try something new, to meet new people, and to practice teamwork and responsibility. For those reasons, I support the principal's decision, and I believe our school will be a stronger community because of it.
